source.title: PANDA: Preference Adaptation for Enhancing Domain-Specific Abilities of LLMs
source.authors: An Liu; Zong-Han Yang; Zhenhe Zhang; Qing-Yuan Hu; Peng Li; Ming Yan; Ji Zhang; Fei Huang; Yang Liu

page_placements.theme: In-context weak-to-strong: weak-labelled examples, critiques of weak errors or a weaker expert's insights given as demonstrations

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares a strong general-purpose LLM using expert-derived preferences with weaker domain expert models, but uses inference-time retrieved insights rather than fine-tuning on weak labels. Its task scores therefore bear on the conceptual weak-to-strong effect, not on the original fine-tuning recipe.
record.gate_note: PANDA uses GPT-3.5-turbo-1106 to generate and retrieve explanations of preferences from domain experts; it does not fine-tune the strong model on weak labels. The rows record the reported task scores for PANDA against the no-PANDA baseline, with expert scores noted as the weak-supervisor reference. The study does not calculate PGR or a strong-model ceiling.
record.test_reason: PANDA has GPT-3.5-turbo-1106 read, in context, explanations of a small fine-tuned expert's top-2 preferences (flan-t5-large on ScienceWorld, RoBERTa-base on TweetEval). Nothing is fine-tuned on the expert's labels. This is not the weak-to-strong setup the versions describe, for three reasons. (1) The 'weak' supervisor is the stronger party on the task: GPT-3.5 without PANDA scores below the expert on 16/20 ScienceWorld tasks and 5/7 TweetEval tasks. (2) No strong ceiling trained on ground truth is reported, so PGR cannot be computed. (3) The student keeps its own prompting and environment access, so beating the expert cannot be credited to the weak labels. The paper invokes Burns et al. only as an analogy ('similar phenomenon'). The 'student exceeds expert' cases are recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that PANDA, a tuning-free method, improves GPT-3.5 on domain tasks in most cases (ReAct improves on 16/20 ScienceWorld tasks; most TweetEval tasks across 4 prompt settings). They say ReAct+PANDA exceeds the fine-tuned expert on 4 ScienceWorld tasks, which they frame as analogous to weak-to-strong generalization. They also report that PANDA degrades ReAct where ReAct already beat the expert.
record.recipe_differences: PANDA is a tuning-free, retrieval-based in-context method: the LLM explains expert preference pairs, stores the resulting insights, and retrieves them during inference. It does not fine-tune the strong model on weak labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across tasks and TweetEval prompt settings (zero-shot, few-shot, and Chain-of-Thought). The number of retrieved insights is set to 1 for ScienceWorld and 6 for TweetEval; the paper does not report a comparison of those retrieval counts.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-3.5 given in-context insights explaining a small fine-tuned expert's preferences sometimes scores above that expert. ReAct+PANDA exceeds the expert on 4/20 ScienceWorld tasks (e.g. 7-1: 95.5 vs 85.0) where the no-PANDA baseline was below it; on TweetEval this holds only in Climate few-shot (69.1 vs 54.3). Where the baseline LLM already beat the expert (ScienceWorld 2-1, 5-2), PANDA pulled the score toward the expert.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tuning-free (in-context) learning from a task-stronger but generally weaker expert can let a general LLM exceed the expert on some tasks, and can also drag it down toward the expert where the expert is worse.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No PGR is calculated, and no strong ceiling is reported. The main ScienceWorld results use a single strong-model family and task scores; the paper says experiments were run for 5 rounds and averaged, but gives no error bars in the reported tables. The method differs from fine-tuning on weak labels, and only selected tasks are explicitly described as surpassing the expert.
record.rows_left_out: The 40 separate Reflexion-with-PANDA and SayCan-with-PANDA ScienceWorld task scores in Table 1 were omitted due to the 60-row limit; the chosen rows retain all 20 ReAct-with-PANDA task scores and all 28 PANDA TweetEval scores. Additional ablation, cross-task transfer, and data-quality scores in Tables 3–9 were omitted because they evaluate PANDA variants or auxiliary comparisons rather than the principal weak-expert versus strong-model outcomes recorded here.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on weak labels, no strong ceiling, no PGR. The supervisor is usually task-stronger than the student.
No auxiliary loss, ensembling or loss variants. The PANDA ablations compare prompting variants, not PGR.
Single student and no size sweep. No PGR by task, no representation predictors.
No tests of supervisor-blind-spot exploitation or correlated errors. The cross-task transfer tests (Tables 4–5) report no PGR.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's states used 'reversed' for 'PANDA below expert' and 'observed' for 'above expert', even where the baseline LLM already beat the expert. Both readings are invalid for V1, so all rows are relinked to none. The paper's 'weak' refers to general capability, not task skill. ScienceWorld scores are 5-run averages with no error bars. The Reflexion and SayCan columns, also omitted from the rows, show the same pattern: no ceiling, supervisor task-stronger.

versions.untested_parts: Tests whether a strong model using expert-derived preferences can exceed the expert on task outcomes, but not fine-tuning on weak labels or PGR as defined.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, or loss-variant comparison raising PGR.
Reports task-dependent outcomes for a fixed GPT-3.5 model and domain experts; does not sweep student or supervisor size, calculate PGR, or analyze representations as predictors.
Does not test exploitability of supervisor blind spots, distribution shift as a cause of reduced PGR, or correlated student-supervisor errors.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.

relation.reason: The authors explicitly compare PANDA with weak-to-strong generalization and discuss tuning-free extensions, without testing the catalog's claim versions.

tranche.reason: PANDA retrieves explanations of expert preferences into the inference context. It neither fine-tunes the student on weak labels nor tests another listed claim version; its results measure a related construct.

source_check.notes: The four highlighted ScienceWorld tasks cross from below to above the expert; other tasks already exceed the expert without PANDA. Appendix B reports ScienceWorld scores averaged over five rounds, without uncertainty estimates.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ReAct with PANDA on ScienceWorld Tasks 3-4, 6-1, 7-1, and 7-3; selected TweetEval stance conditions
reader_labels.reason: PANDA scores exceed the reported expert score in these settings (SW-R-3-4, SW-R-6-1, SW-R-7-1, SW-R-7-3, TE-Abortion-ZS, TE-Abortion-FS, TE-Climate-ZS, TE-Climate-FS, TE-Abortion-FSCoT, TE-Climate-FSCoT). This is an in-context adaptation result, not fine-tuning or PGR.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Other listed ScienceWorld and TweetEval task/prompt settings
reader_labels.reason: The PANDA model remains below the expert on many tasks, despite sometimes improving over its no-PANDA baseline; the effect is not consistent across tasks and prompts (rows linked to V1 outside the supports group).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tested ScienceWorld tasks and TweetEval task/prompt conditions
reader_labels.reason: Outcomes vary by task and prompt setting, and surpassing the domain expert occurs in only some of the reported settings; the study does not sweep model size or report PGR (rows SW-R-1-1 through SW-R-10-2 and TE-Emoji-ZS through TE-Sentiment-FSCoT).
